arXiv:quant-ph/0304007v2 [quant-ph] 22 Aug 2003

Structure of states which satisfy strong subadditivity
of quantum entropy with equality

Patrick Hayden Email: patrick@cs.caltech.edu Affiliation: Institute for Quantum Information, Caltech 107–81, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA    Richard Jozsa Email: richard@cs.bris.ac.uk Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Bristol,
Merchant Venturers Building, Woodland Road, Bristol BS8 1UB, United Kingdom    Dénes Petz Email: petz@math.bme.hu Affiliation: Department for Mathematical Analysis, Mathematical Institute,
Budapest University of Technology and Economics, Egry József utca 2, H–1111 Budapest, Hungary    Andreas Winter Email: winter@cs.bris.ac.uk Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Bristol,
Merchant Venturers Building, Woodland Rd, Bristol BS8 1UB, United Kingdom
22nd August 2003
Abstract

We give an explicit characterisation of the quantum states which saturate the strong subadditivity inequality for the von Neumann entropy. By combining a result of Petz characterising the equality case for the monotonicity of relative entropy with a recent theorem by Koashi and Imoto, we show that such states will have the form of a so–called short quantum Markov chain, which in turn implies that two of the systems are independent conditioned on the third, in a physically meaningful sense. This characterisation simultaneously generalises known necessary and sufficient entropic conditions for quantum error correction as well as the conditions for the achievability of the Holevo bound on accessible information.

Keywords: 
Entropy, strong subadditivity, invariant algebras, quantum Markov state

I Introduction

The von Neumann entropy [13]

S⁡(ρ)=−Tr⁡ρ​log⁡ρ,S(\rho)=-{\operatorname{Tr}}\rho\log\rho,

of a density operator ρ\rho on a finite dimensional Hilbert space ℋ{\cal H} shares many properties with its classical counterpart, the Shannon entropy

H(P)=−∑x∈𝒳P(x)logP(x)H(P)=-\sum_{x\in{\mathcal{X}}}P(x)\log P(x)

of a probability distribution PP on a discrete set 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}. (All logarithms in this work are understood to be to base 22. Also, we will use the terms “state” and “density operator” interchangeably.) For example, both are nonnegative, and equal to 00 if and only if the state (distribution) is an extreme point in the set of all states (distributions), i.e. if ρ\rho is pure (PP is a point mass). Both are concave and, moreover, both are subadditive: for a state ρA​B\rho_{AB} on a composite system ℋA⊗ℋB{\cal H}_{A}\otimes{\cal H}_{B} with reduced states

ρA=TrB⁡(ρA​B),ρB=TrA⁡(ρA​B),\rho_{A}={\operatorname{Tr}}_{B}\bigl(\rho_{AB}\bigr),\quad\rho_{B}={\operatorname{Tr}}_{A}\bigl(\rho_{AB}\bigr),

it holds that

S⁡(ρA​B)≤S⁡(ρA)+S⁡(ρB).S(\rho_{AB})\leq S(\rho_{A})+S(\rho_{B}).

A directly analogous inequality holds for a distribution over a product set and its marginals. (Many more properties of SS are collected in the review by Wehrl [26] and in the monograph [14].)

We shall view von Neumann entropy as a generalisation of Shannon entropy [19] in the following precise way: if the set 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} labels an orthonormal basis {|x⟩:x∈𝒳}\bigl\{{|{x}\rangle}:x\in{\mathcal{X}}\bigr\} of ℋX{\cal H}_{X} we can construct the state

ρP=∑xP⁡(x)​|x⟩​⟨x|\rho_{P}=\sum_{x}P(x){{|{x}\rangle}\!{\langle{x}|}}

corresponding to the distribution PP. This clearly defines an affine linear map from distributions into states. It is then straightforward to check that

S⁡(ρP)=H⁡(P),S(\rho_{P})=H(P),

so all properties of von Neumann entropy of a single system also hold for Shannon entropy of a single distribution.

Similarly, for a distribution PP on a cartesian product 𝒳×𝒴{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}}, we use the tensor product basis

{|xy⟩=|x⟩⊗|y⟩:x∈𝒳,y∈𝒴}\bigl\{{|{xy}\rangle}={|{x}\rangle}\otimes{|{y}\rangle}:x\in{\mathcal{X}},y\in{\mathcal{Y}}\bigr\}

to define the state ρP\rho_{P} on ℋX⊗ℋY{\cal H}_{X}\otimes{\cal H}_{Y}. Again, it is straightforward to check that reduced states correspond to taking marginals:

TrY⁡(ρP)=ρP|𝒳,TrX⁡(ρP)=ρP|𝒴.{\operatorname{Tr}}_{Y}\bigl(\rho_{P}\bigr)=\rho_{P|_{{\mathcal{X}}}},\quad{\operatorname{Tr}}_{X}\bigl(\rho_{P}\bigr)=\rho_{P|_{{\mathcal{Y}}}}.

Hence all entropy relations for bipartite states also hold for bipartite distributions.

In [9] Lieb and Ruskai proved the remarkable relation

S⁡(ρA​B)+S⁡(ρB​C)≥S⁡(ρA​B​C)+S⁡(ρB),S(\rho_{AB})+S(\rho_{BC})\geq S(\rho_{ABC})+S(\rho_{B}), (1)

with a tripartite state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} on the system ℋA⊗ℋB⊗ℋC{\cal H}_{A}\otimes{\cal H}_{B}\otimes{\cal H}_{C}. It clearly generalises the previous subadditivity relation, which is recovered for a trivial system BB: ℋB=ℂ{\cal H}_{B}={\mathbb{C}}. In fact, this inequality plays a crucial role in nearly every nontrivial insight in quantum information theory, from the famous Holevo bound [5] and the properties of the coherent information [3, 18] to the recently proved additivity of capacity for entanglement–breaking channels [20].

The present investigation aims to resolve the problem of characterising the states which satisfy this relation with equality: the main result is theorem 6. Roughly speaking, the strong subadditivity inequality expresses the fact that discarding a subsystem of a quantum system is a dissipative operation, in the sense that it can only destroy correlations with the rest of the world. Our work, therefore, can be interpreted as providing a detailed description of the conditions under which the act of discarding a quantum system can be locally reversed on a particular input. We restrict ourselves to finite dimensional systems in this paper. The question of whether a similar result holds in infinite dimension is left open.

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. In section II we will review the case of probability distributions: there the solution to our problem is easy to obtain, and in fact well–known. This will provide the intuitive basis for understanding our main result. After that, in section III we review quantum relative entropy and the relation of its monotonicity property to the strong subadditivity inequality. Section IV presents a condition given by Petz for equality in the monotonicity of relative entropy, while section V presents and proves our main result, a structure theorem for states which satisfy strong subadditivity with equality. An essential step is the application of a recent result of Koashi and Imoto [7] for which we give a short but non–constructive algebraic proof in the appendix. In section VI, we show how the entropic conditions for quantum error correction as well as the conditions for saturation in the Holevo bound follow as easy corollaries from our structure theorem.

The question of characterising the equality case of strong subadditivity as well as of the monotonicity of relative entropy was considered in earlier work by Petz [15], where it was related to the existence of quantum operations with certain properties. Ruskai [17] has given a characterisation in terms of an operator equality, which can be used to show that the states described in our main theorem 6 are indeed equality cases (as she has informed us, this was pointed out to her by M. A. Nielsen after [17] appeared). Neither of these results is as explicit as one could wish for, however, because while both give algebraic criteria which one can check on any given state, they do not yield a simple description of all the states that satisfy equality. This simple description is exactly what our theorem 6 provides.

II The classical case

Let us first look at the classical case of probability distributions and their Shannon entropies. The exposition is most conveniently phrased in terms of random variables denoted A,B,CA,B,C, taking values in 𝒜,ℬ,𝒞{\cal A,B,C}, respectively, with a joint distribution

PA​B​C​(a,b,c)=Pr⁡{A=a,B=b,C=c}.P_{ABC}(a,b,c)=\Pr\{A=a,B=b,C=c\}.

The distribution of AA is the marginal PA=PA​B​C|𝒜P_{A}=P_{ABC}|_{\cal A} of the joint distribution to 𝒜{\cal A} and similarly for the other variables.

Shannon [19] defined the mutual information

I⁡(A:B)=H⁡(A)+H⁡(B)−H⁡(A​B),I(A:B)=H(A)+H(B)-H(AB),

with H⁡(A)=H⁡(PA)H(A)=H(P_{A}) and so on. It is not hard to show that I⁡(A:B)≥0I(A:B)\geq 0 with equality if and only if AA and BB are independent.

Conditional mutual information is defined as

I(A:C|B)=∑b∈ℬPB(b)I(A:C|B=b),I(A:C|B)=\sum_{b\in{\cal B}}P_{B}(b)I(A:C|B=b),

where I(A:C|B=b)I(A:C|B=b) is the mutual information between the variables AA and CC conditional on the event “B=bB=b”, i.e. I⁡(A|B=b:C|B=b)I(A|_{B=b}:C|_{B=b}), with

Pr⁡{A|B=b=a,C|B=b=c}=PA​B​C​(a,b,c)PB​(b)=:PA​C|B​(a,c|b).\begin{split}\Pr\bigl\{A|_{B=b}=a,C|_{B=b}=c\bigr\}&=\frac{P_{ABC}(a,b,c)}{P_{B}(b)}\\ &=:P_{AC|B}(a,c|b).\end{split}

It is straightforward to check that with these definitions one has the chain rule

I(A:BC)=I(A:B)+I(A:C|B).I(A:BC)=I(A:B)+I(A:C|B). (2)

This implies the formula

I(A:C|B)=H(AB)+H(BC)−H(ABC)−H(B).I(A:C|B)=H(AB)+H(BC)-H(ABC)-H(B).

Because the left hand side is by definition a convex combination of mutual informations, each of which is always nonnegative, we obtain strong subadditivity for classical distributions.

Theorem 1

I(A:C|B)=0I(A:C|B)=0 if and only if AA and CC are conditionally independent given BB, meaning

∀b​ s.t. ​PB​(b)≠0A|B=b,C|B=b​ are independent.\forall b\text{ s.t. }P_{B}(b)\neq 0\quad A|_{B=b},C|_{B=b}\text{ are independent.}

This is the case if and only if

PA​B​C​(a,b,c)=PB​(b)​PA|B​(a|b)​PC|B​(c|b)=PA​(a)​PB|A​(b|a)​PC|B​(c|b),\begin{split}P_{ABC}(a,b,c)&=P_{B}(b)P_{A|B}(a|b)P_{C|B}(c|b)\\ &=P_{A}(a)P_{B|A}(b|a)P_{C|B}(c|b),\end{split} (3)

i.e. iff AA—BB—CC is a Markov chain in this order.

Proof . Clearly, the conditions are sufficient. Assume conversely that I(A:C|B)=0I(A:C|B)=0. By definition of the latter quantity, this implies that for all bb with PB​(b)≠0P_{B}(b)\neq 0, I(A:C|B=b)=0I(A:C|B=b)=0. But this implies independence of A|B=bA|_{B=b} and C|B=bC|_{B=b}. Hence, eq. (3) follows:

PA​B​C​(a,b,c)=PB​(b)​PA​C|B​(a,c|b)=PB​(b)​PA|B​(a|b)​PC|B​(c|b)=PA​(a)​PB|A​(b|a)​PC|B​(c|b).\begin{split}P_{ABC}(a,b,c)&=P_{B}(b)P_{AC|B}(a,c|b)\\ &=P_{B}(b)P_{A|B}(a|b)P_{C|B}(c|b)\\ &=P_{A}(a)P_{B|A}(b|a)P_{C|B}(c|b).\end{split}

□\Box

The remainder of the paper is devoted to describing the quantum mechanical generalisation of this equivalence between zero conditional mutual information, conditional independence, the Markov property and the factorization of the joint distribution given in eq. (3).

III Relative entropy

Our approach to saturation of the strong subaddivity inequality will be via the quantum relative entropy; this quantity was defined by Umegaki [25] for two quantum states ρ\rho and σ\sigma as

S(ρ∥σ)=Tr(ρ(logρ−logσ))S(\rho\|\sigma)={\operatorname{Tr}}\bigl(\rho(\log\rho-\log\sigma)\bigr)

if the support of ρ\rho is contained in the support of σ\sigma, and +∞+\infty otherwise. We note that this definition generalises the familiar Kullback–Leibler divergence [8] of two probability distributions, just as von Neumann entropy generalises Shannon entropy.

For a bipartite state ρA​B\rho_{AB} it is straightforward to check that

S(ρA​B∥ρA⊗ρB)=S(ρA)+S(ρB)−S(ρA​B),S(\rho_{AB}\|\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B})=S(\rho_{A})+S(\rho_{B})-S(\rho_{AB}), (4)

and the latter quantity is abbreviated I⁡(A:B)I(A:B), in formal extension of the definition of Shannon’s mutual information [19] to quantum states.

Example 2

Let {p⁡(x),ρx}\{p(x),\rho_{x}\} be an ensemble of quantum states on ℋ{\cal H}. The Holevo quantity χ\chi is defined as

χ⁡({p⁡(x),ρx})=S⁡(∑xp⁡(x)​ρx)−∑xp⁡(x)​S​(ρx).\chi\bigl(\{p(x),\rho_{x}\}\bigr)=S\left(\sum_{x}p(x)\rho_{x}\right)-\sum_{x}p(x)S(\rho_{x}).

Holevo [5] showed that this quantity is an upper bound to the mutual information between xx and the outcomes yy of any particular measurement performed on the states ρx\rho_{x}.

It is easily seen that

χ⁡({p⁡(x),ρx})=I⁡(A:B),\chi\bigl(\{p(x),\rho_{x}\}\bigr)=I(A:B),

with the bipartite state

ρA​B=∑xp⁡(x)​|x⟩​⟨x|A⊗(ρx)B.\rho_{AB}=\sum_{x}p(x){{|{x}\rangle}\!{\langle{x}|}}_{A}\otimes(\rho_{x})_{B}.

For a tripartite state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} we can also consider the information I⁡(A:B​C)I(A:BC), which can be written as

S(ρA​B​C∥ρA⊗ρB​C)=S(ρA)+S(ρB​C)−S(ρA​B​C).S(\rho_{ABC}\|\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{BC})=S(\rho_{A})+S(\rho_{BC})-S(\rho_{ABC}). (5)

The difference between eqs. (5) and (4), which by virtue of the classical chain rule eq. (2) we might call the quantum conditional mutual information I(A:C|B)I(A:C|B) is, therefore,

S(ρA​B​C∥ρA⊗ρB​C)−S(ρA​B∥ρA⊗ρB)=S⁡(ρA​B)+S⁡(ρB​C)−S⁡(ρA​B​C)−S⁡(ρB).\begin{split}S(\rho_{ABC}\|\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{BC})&-S(\rho_{AB}\|\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B})\\ &\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!=S(\rho_{AB})+S(\rho_{BC})-S(\rho_{ABC})-S(\rho_{B}).\end{split} (6)

The right hand side here is nonnegative by strong subadditivity. (Note that this is an important theorem in the quantum case despite being an almost trivial observation classically.) The left hand side, however, can be rewritten as S(ρ∥σ)−S(Tρ∥Tσ)S(\rho\|\sigma)-S(T\rho\|T\sigma), with the states ρ=ρA​B​C\rho=\rho_{ABC} and σ=ρA⊗ρB​C\sigma=\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{BC}, and the quantum operation T=TrCT={\operatorname{Tr}}_{C}, the partial trace over ℋC{\cal H}_{C}, which as a linear map can be written as T=idA​B⊗TrT={\operatorname{id}}_{AB}\otimes{\operatorname{Tr}}.

Now a theorem of Uhlmann [24] (proved earlier by Lindblad [10] for the finite–dimensional case of interest here) says that for all states ρ\rho and σ\sigma on a space ℋ{\cal H}, and all quantum operations T:ℬ⁡(ℋ)→ℬ⁡(𝒦)T:{\cal B}({\cal H})\rightarrow{\cal B}({\cal K}),

S(ρ∥σ)≥S(Tρ∥Tσ),S(\rho\|\sigma)\geq S(T\rho\|T\sigma), (7)

so Uhlmann’s theorem implies strong subadditivity and we have equality in the latter if and only if there is equality in the former.

IV The equality condition
for relative entropy

The formulation in the previous section of strong subadditivity as a relative entropy monotonicity under a partial trace operation transforms the question for the equality conditions for the former into the same question for the latter. Note that by the very monotonicity relation, there is a “trivial” case of equality in eq. (7), namely if there exists a quantum operation T^\widehat{T} mapping T​ρT\rho to ρ\rho and T​σT\sigma to σ\sigma. In fact, this is the only case of equality:

Theorem 3 (Petz [15])

For states ρ\rho and σ\sigma,

S(ρ∥σ)=S(Tρ∥Tσ)S(\rho\|\sigma)=S(T\rho\|T\sigma)

if and only if there exists a quantum operation T^\widehat{T} such that

T^​T​ρ=ρ,T^​T​σ=σ.\widehat{T}T\rho=\rho,\quad\widehat{T}T\sigma=\sigma.

Furthermore, on the support of T​σT\sigma, T^\widehat{T} can be given explicitly by the formula

T^​α=σ12​T∗​((T​σ)−12​α​(T​σ)−12)​σ12,\widehat{T}\alpha=\sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}T^{*}\left((T\sigma)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\alpha(T\sigma)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\sigma^{\frac{1}{2}}, (8)

with the adjoint map T∗T^{*} of TT:

T∗​(X)=∑iAi∗​X​Ai, if ​T​(α)=∑iAi​α​Ai∗.T^{*}(X)=\sum_{i}A_{i}^{*}XA_{i},\text{ if }T(\alpha)=\sum_{i}A_{i}\alpha A_{i}^{*}.

□\Box

Observe that the definition of T^\widehat{T} in eq. (8) depends on σ\sigma, thereby automatically ensuring that T^​T​σ=σ\widehat{T}T\sigma=\sigma. Sometimes, we add the subscript σ\sigma to T^\widehat{T} to emphasize the dependence.

Example 4

As in example 2, let {p⁡(x),ρx}\{p(x),\rho_{x}\} be an ensemble of states on ℋ{\cal H} and define

ρA​B=∑xp⁡(x)​|x⟩​⟨x|A⊗(ρx)B.\rho_{AB}=\sum_{x}p(x){{|{x}\rangle}\!{\langle{x}|}}_{A}\otimes(\rho_{x})_{B}.

There we observed that, with σ=ρA⊗ρB\sigma=\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B},

χ({p(x),ρx})=S(ρ∥σ).\chi\bigl(\{p(x),\rho_{x}\}\bigr)=S(\rho\|\sigma).

Now, let φ\varphi be a quantum operation on ℋ{\cal H} (which could be a measurement), and form T=idA⊗φBT={\operatorname{id}}_{A}\otimes\varphi_{B}. Then

χ⁡({p⁡(x),ρx})=S(ρA​B∥ρA⊗ρB)≥S(TρA​B∥T(ρA⊗ρB))=χ⁡({p⁡(x),φ​ρx}),\begin{split}\chi\bigl(\{p(x),\rho_{x}\}\bigr)&=S(\rho_{AB}\|\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B})\\ &\geq S\bigl(T\rho_{AB}\|T(\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B})\bigr)\\ &=\chi\bigl(\{p(x),\varphi\rho_{x}\}\bigr),\end{split} (9)

which is (a generalistion of) the famous Holevo bound [5] in the form of a data processing relation.

Equality holds, according to theorem 3, if and only if T^\widehat{T} of eq. (8) maps T​ρT\rho to ρ\rho. Note that we may assume without loss of generality that σ=ρA⊗ρB\sigma=\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B} is strictly positive. But it is straightforward to check that

T^σ=id^ρA⊗φ^ρB=id⊗φ^,\widehat{T}_{\sigma}=\widehat{{\operatorname{id}}}_{\rho_{A}}\otimes\widehat{\varphi}_{\rho_{B}}={\operatorname{id}}\otimes\widehat{\varphi},

hence we have equality in eq. (9) if and only if for all xx, φ^​φ​ρx=ρx\widehat{\varphi}\varphi\rho_{x}=\rho_{x}.

Remark 5

In [2] the “transpose channel” T^\widehat{T} of eq. (8), as it is called in [14], makes an appearance in a slightly different context: there a set of states is subjected to a quantum channel, and the problem is to find the best recovery map which maximises a fidelity criterion for the original states and the images of the channel output states. It was shown that the error using T^\widehat{T} is always at most twice as the minimum error under the optimal recovery map.

V Structure of states with equality

Let ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} be a state on ℋA⊗ℋB⊗ℋC{\cal H}_{A}\otimes{\cal H}_{B}\otimes{\cal H}_{C}. As we observed earlier, Uhlmann’s theorem specialized to the states ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} and σA​B​C=ρA⊗ρB​C\sigma_{ABC}=\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{BC}, along with the map T=TrCT={\operatorname{Tr}}_{C}, states that

S(ρA​B​C∥ρA⊗ρB​C)≥S(ρA​B∥ρA⊗ρB).S(\rho_{ABC}\|\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{BC})\geq S(\rho_{AB}\|\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B}).

Consequently, theorem 3 provides the condition for equality here: T^​T​ρ=ρ\widehat{T}T\rho=\rho. Now, because T=idA⊗RB​CT={\operatorname{id}}_{A}\otimes R_{BC}, with the restriction map RB​C=idB⊗TrCR_{BC}={\operatorname{id}}_{B}\otimes{\operatorname{Tr}}_{C}, and σ\sigma is a tensor product, we obtain (compare example 4):

T^=idA⊗R^,\widehat{T}={\operatorname{id}}_{A}\otimes\widehat{R}, (10)

with R^=R^ρB​C\widehat{R}=\widehat{R}_{\rho_{BC}}.

Summarising, in the above monotonicity and hence in strong subadditivity we have equality if and only if

ρA​B​C=(id⊗R^)​ρA​B.\rho_{ABC}=({\operatorname{id}}\otimes\widehat{R})\rho_{AB}. (11)

We are now in a position to prove our main result:

Theorem 6

A state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} on ℋA⊗ℋB⊗ℋC{\cal H}_{A}\otimes{\cal H}_{B}\otimes{\cal H}_{C} satisfies strong subadditivity (eq. (1)) with equality if and only if there is a decomposition of system BB as

ℋB=⨁jℋbjL⊗ℋbjR{\cal H}_{B}=\bigoplus_{j}{\cal H}_{b^{L}_{j}}\otimes{\cal H}_{b^{R}_{j}}

into a direct sum of tensor products, such that

ρA​B​C=⨁jqj​ρA​bjL⊗ρbjR​C,\rho_{ABC}=\bigoplus_{j}q_{j}\rho_{Ab^{L}_{j}}\otimes\rho_{b^{R}_{j}C},

with states ρA​bjL\rho_{Ab^{L}_{j}} on ℋA⊗ℋbjL{\cal H}_{A}\otimes{\cal H}_{b^{L}_{j}} and ρbjR​C\rho_{b^{R}_{j}C} on ℋbjR⊗ℋC{\cal H}_{b^{R}_{j}}\otimes{\cal H}_{C}, and a probability distribution {qj}\{q_{j}\}.

Proof . The sufficiency of the condition is immediate. The proof of necessity will come from analysing the quantum Markov chain condition, eq. (11).

After defining the quantum operation φ=TrC∘R^\varphi={\operatorname{Tr}}_{C}\circ\widehat{R}, the Markov condition gives us

(id⊗φ)​ρA​B=ρA​B.({\operatorname{id}}\otimes\varphi)\rho_{AB}=\rho_{AB}. (12)

Consider an operator MM on ℋA{\cal H}_{A} with 0≤M≤𝟙0\leq M\leq{\openone}, and define a state μ\mu by

p​μ=TrA⁡(ρA​B​(M⊗𝟙)),p=Tr⁡(ρA​B​(M⊗𝟙)).p\mu={\operatorname{Tr}}_{A}\bigl(\rho_{AB}(M\otimes{\openone})\bigr),\ p={\operatorname{Tr}}\bigl(\rho_{AB}(M\otimes{\openone})\bigr).

Then, if p≠0p\neq 0, eq. (12) implies that φ⁡(μ)=μ\varphi(\mu)=\mu. Varying the operator MM we obtain a family 𝐌{\bf M} of states on ℋA{\cal H}_{A} invariant under φ\varphi.

To this we can apply theorem 10 from the appendix. We obtain a decomposition

ℋB=⨁jℋbjL⊗ℋbjR,{\cal H}_{B}=\bigoplus_{j}{\cal H}_{b^{L}_{j}}\otimes{\cal H}_{b^{R}_{j}}, (13)

such that every μ∈𝐌\mu\in{\bf M} can be written

μ=⨁jqj​(μ)​ρj​(μ)⊗ωj,\mu=\bigoplus_{j}q_{j}(\mu)\rho_{j}(\mu)\otimes\omega_{j},

with states ρj​(μ)\rho_{j}(\mu) on ℋbjL{\cal H}_{b^{L}_{j}} and ωj\omega_{j} on ℋbjR{\cal H}_{b^{R}_{j}}. This, in turn, easily implies the following structure for ρA​B\rho_{AB}:

ρA​B=⨁jqj​ρA​bjL⊗ωbjR.\rho_{AB}=\bigoplus_{j}q_{j}\rho_{Ab^{L}_{j}}\otimes\omega_{b^{R}_{j}}. (14)

To see this, introduce the quantum operation

P0​(ξ)=⨁jTrbjR⁡(Πj​ξ​Πj)⊗ωj,P_{0}(\xi)=\bigoplus_{j}{\operatorname{Tr}}_{b^{R}_{j}}\bigl(\Pi_{j}\xi\Pi_{j}\bigr)\otimes\omega_{j},

on ℋB{\cal H}_{B}, where Πj\Pi_{j} is the orthogonal projector onto the subspace ℋbjL⊗ℋbjR{\cal H}_{b^{L}_{j}}\otimes{\cal H}_{b^{R}_{j}} in eq. (13). (Its dual P0∗P_{0}^{*} is the subalgebra projection from the appendix, where it is denoted the same way.) Then it is easy to calculate, for arbitrary operators MM and NN bounded between 00 and 𝟙{\openone}:

Tr⁡(ρA​B​(M⊗N))=p​Tr⁡(μ​N)=p​Tr⁡(P0​(μ)​N)=p​Tr⁡(μ​P0∗​(N))=Tr⁡(ρA​B​(M⊗P0∗​(N)))=Tr⁡(((id⊗P0)​ρA​B)​(M⊗N)).\begin{split}{\operatorname{Tr}}\bigl(\rho_{AB}(M\otimes N)\bigr)&=p{\operatorname{Tr}}(\mu N)\\ &=p{\operatorname{Tr}}\bigl(P_{0}(\mu)N\bigr)\\ &=p{\operatorname{Tr}}\bigl(\mu P_{0}^{*}(N)\bigr)\\ &={\operatorname{Tr}}\Bigl(\rho_{AB}\bigl(M\otimes P_{0}^{*}(N)\bigr)\Bigr)\\ &={\operatorname{Tr}}\Bigl(\bigl(({\operatorname{id}}\otimes P_{0})\rho_{AB}\bigr)(M\otimes N)\bigr).\\ \end{split}

By linearity, this holds for all operators in place of M⊗NM\otimes N, so

ρA​B=(id⊗P0)​ρA​B,\rho_{AB}=({\operatorname{id}}\otimes P_{0})\rho_{AB},

implying eq. (14), because

(id⊗P0)​ξ=⨁jTrbjR⁡((𝟙⊗Πj)​ξ​(𝟙⊗Πj∗))⊗ωj.({\operatorname{id}}\otimes P_{0})\xi=\bigoplus_{j}{\operatorname{Tr}}_{b^{R}_{j}}\bigl(({\openone}\otimes\Pi_{j})\xi({\openone}\otimes\Pi_{j}^{*})\bigr)\otimes\omega_{j}.

But theorem 10 also gives information about φ\varphi: introduce an environment ℋE{\cal H}_{E} in state ε\varepsilon and a unitary UU on ℋB⊗ℋC⊗ℋE{\cal H}_{B}\otimes{\cal H}_{C}\otimes{\cal H}_{E} such that

R^​(α)=TrE⁡(U⁡(α⊗|0⟩​⟨0|⊗ε)​U∗),\widehat{R}(\alpha)={\operatorname{Tr}}_{E}\bigl(U(\alpha\otimes{{|{0}\rangle}\!{\langle{0}|}}\otimes\varepsilon)U^{*}\bigr),

with a standard state |0⟩∈ℋC{|{0}\rangle}\in{\cal H}_{C}. Because a further trace over CC gives us φ\varphi, we obtain the following form for UU (with ℰ=ℋC⊗ℋE{\cal E}={\cal H}_{C}\otimes{\cal H}_{E}):

U=⨁j𝟙ℋbjL⊗Uj,U=\bigoplus_{j}{\openone}_{{\cal H}_{b^{L}_{j}}}\otimes U_{j}, (15)

with UjU_{j} a unitary on ℋbjR⊗ℰ{\cal H}_{b^{R}_{j}}\otimes{\cal E}.

Putting eqs. (14) and (15) together, we finally get:

ρA​B​C=(idA⊗R^)​ρA​B=TrE⁡((𝟙A⊗U)​ρA​B​(𝟙A⊗U∗))=⨁jqj​ρA​bjL⊗TrE⁡(U⁡(ωbjR⊗|0⟩​⟨0|)​U∗)=⨁jqj​ρA​bjL⊗ρbjR​C,\begin{split}\rho_{ABC}&=({\operatorname{id}}_{A}\otimes\widehat{R})\rho_{AB}\\ &={\operatorname{Tr}}_{E}\bigl(({\openone}_{A}\otimes U)\rho_{AB}({\openone}_{A}\otimes U^{*})\bigr)\\ &=\bigoplus_{j}q_{j}\rho_{Ab^{L}_{j}}\otimes{\operatorname{Tr}}_{E}\bigl(U(\omega_{b^{R}_{j}}\otimes{{|{0}\rangle}\!{\langle{0}|}})U^{*}\bigr)\\ &=\bigoplus_{j}q_{j}\rho_{Ab^{L}_{j}}\otimes\rho_{b^{R}_{j}C},\end{split}

which is what we wanted to prove. □\Box

Quantum Markov states on the infinite tensor product of matrix algebras ⨂i=−∞∞Mn​(ℂ)(i)\bigotimes_{i=-\infty}^{\infty}M_{n}({{\mathbb{C}}})^{(i)} were introduced by Accardi and Frigerio [1]. Let 𝒜m{\cal A}_{m} be the subproduct of the factors with superscript i≤mi\leq m. Then 𝒜m⊂𝒜m+1{\cal A}_{m}\subset{\cal A}_{m+1}. A state ρ\rho of the infinite tensorproduct is called Markovian if for every integer mm there exists a unital completely positive mapping Tm,m+1:𝒜m+1→𝒜mT_{m,m+1}:{\cal A}_{m+1}\rightarrow{\cal A}_{m} which leaves the state ρ\rho (restricted to 𝒜m{\cal A}_{m}) invariant and the subalgebra 𝒜m−1{\cal A}_{m-1} fixed. Accardi and Frigerio call the mapping ℰm,m+1{\cal E}_{m,m+1} quasi–conditional expectation; its dual is the quantum analogue of the Markov kernel in classical probability theory.

Assume that 𝒜m−1=ℬ⁡(ℋA){\cal A}_{m-1}={\cal B}({\cal H}_{A}), Mn​(ℂ)(m)=ℬ⁡(ℋB)M_{n}({{\mathbb{C}}})^{(m)}={\cal B}({\cal H}_{B}) and Mn​(ℂ)(m+1)=ℬ⁡(ℋC)M_{n}({{\mathbb{C}}})^{(m+1)}={\cal B}({\cal H}_{C}). If the equality in strong subadditivity is satisfied in this setting, then we have eq. (10) and the dual of T^\widehat{T} is a quasi–conditional expectation. Therefore the equality in strong subadditivity for every mm yields a quantum Markov state on the infinite system. This property characterises quantum Markov states, see e.g. [14], p. 201.

We propose to call a state as in eq. (11) a short quantum Markov chain (as opposed to the infinite chains introduced in [1]), since we require the existence of the quasi–conditional expectation only for ℬ⁡(ℋA⊗ℋB⊗ℋC)→ℬ⁡(ℋA⊗ℋB){\cal B}({\cal H}_{A}\otimes{\cal H}_{B}\otimes{\cal H}_{C})\rightarrow{\cal B}({\cal H}_{A}\otimes{\cal H}_{B}); note that the analogous quasi–conditional expectation ℬ⁡(ℋA⊗ℋB)→ℬ⁡(ℋA){\cal B}({\cal H}_{A}\otimes{\cal H}_{B})\rightarrow{\cal B}({\cal H}_{A}) exists trivially because the subalgebra to be left invariant is ℂ{\mathbb{C}}.

Corollary 7

For a state ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} satisfying strong subadditivity with equality:

I(A:C|B)=S(ρA​B)+S(ρB​C)−S(ρA​B​C)−S(ρB)=0,I(A:C|B)=S(\rho_{AB})+S(\rho_{BC})-S(\rho_{ABC})-S(\rho_{B})=0,

the marginal state ρA​C\rho_{AC} is separable.

Conversely, for each separable state ρA​C\rho_{AC} there exists an extension ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} such that I(A:C|B)=0I(A:C|B)=0. □\Box

Tucci [23] has given a criterion for separability based on quantum conditional mutual information. Our above result shows that in his Theorem 1, only conditions 1 and 2 are needed, while 3 and 4 are redundant.

VI Applications

Theorem 6 provides a convenient framework for synthesizing many previously known facts in quantum information theory. To illustrate the method of its application, we present a couple of special cases from the literature.

Example 8

The fundamental problem in quantum error correction is to determine when the effect of a quantum operation φ\varphi acting on half of a pure entangled state can be perfectly reversed. Define the coherent information

Ic​(σ,φ)=S⁡(φ​σ)−S⁡((idA⊗φ)​Φσ),I_{c}(\sigma,\varphi)=S(\varphi\sigma)-S\bigl(({\operatorname{id}}_{A}\otimes\varphi)\Phi_{\sigma}\bigr),

where Φσ\Phi_{\sigma} is any purification of σ\sigma to system AA. In [18] it was shown that there exists a quantum operation φ^\hat{\varphi} such that

(idA⊗φ^​φ)​Φσ=Φσ({\operatorname{id}}_{A}\otimes\hat{\varphi}\varphi)\Phi_{\sigma}=\Phi_{\sigma}

if and only if

Ic​(σ,φ)=S⁡(σ).I_{c}(\sigma,\varphi)=S(\sigma). (16)

By the Stinespring dilatation theorem [21], we may assume that

φ​σ=TrC⁡(UB​C​(σ⊗ψ)​UB​C∗)\varphi\sigma={\operatorname{Tr}}_{C}\bigl(U_{BC}(\sigma\otimes\psi)U_{BC}^{*}\bigr)

for a unitary operator UB​CU_{BC} and pure state ancilla ψ\psi on system CC. If we let |ω⟩=(𝟙A⊗UB​C)​(|Φσ⟩⊗|ψ⟩){|{\omega}\rangle}=({\openone}_{A}\otimes U_{BC})({|{\Phi_{\sigma}}\rangle}\otimes{|{\psi}\rangle}) then, taking mutual informations with respect to the state ω=|ω⟩​⟨ω|\omega={{|{\omega}\rangle}\!{\langle{\omega}|}},

S⁡(σ)\displaystyle S(\sigma) =I⁡(A:B​C)−S⁡(A)​ and\displaystyle=I(A:BC)-S(A)\text{ and}
Ic​(σ,φ)\displaystyle I_{c}(\sigma,\varphi) =I⁡(A:B)−S⁡(A).\displaystyle=I(A:B)-S(A).

Therefore, eq. (16) holds iff I⁡(A:B​C)=I⁡(A:B)I(A:BC)=I(A:B). By theorem 6, we can conclude that

ω=⨁jqj​ωA​bjL⊗ωbjR​C.\omega=\bigoplus_{j}q_{j}\omega_{Ab_{j}^{L}}\otimes\omega_{b_{j}^{R}C}.

The recovery procedure φ^\hat{\varphi} given the state

(idA⊗φ)​Φσ=TrC⁡ω({\operatorname{id}}_{A}\otimes\varphi)\Phi_{\sigma}={\operatorname{Tr}}_{C}\omega

is then obvious: first measure jj before preparing the state ωbjR​C\omega_{b_{j}^{R}C} on ℋbjR⊗ℋC{\cal H}_{b_{j}^{R}}\otimes{\cal H}_{C}. Next, perform UB​C∗U_{BC}^{*} and discard the fixed ancilla state ψ\psi. The output is exactly Φσ\Phi_{\sigma}. As an aside, the reason that the solution to this problem was accessible without the results of the present paper is that a closer examination of the situation reveals that, because Φσ\Phi_{\sigma} is pure, only the equality conditions for the usual subadditivity inequality are required in the construction of the reversal map. Strong subadditivity, in this case, is superfluous.

Example 9

Returning to our investigation of the Holevo bound from example 4, let {p⁡(x),ρx}\{p(x),\rho_{x}\} be an ensemble of states on ℋ{\cal H}, ρA​B=∑xp⁡(x)​|x⟩​⟨x|A⊗(ρx)B\rho_{AB}=\sum_{x}p(x){{|{x}\rangle}\!{\langle{x}|}}_{A}\otimes(\rho_{x})_{B} and φ\varphi a quantum operation on the BB system. Again by the Stinespring dilation theorem, after possibly adjoining a fixed ancilla and performing a common unitary operation to all the ρx\rho_{x}, we may assume without loss of generality that B=B~​C~B=\tilde{B}\tilde{C} and φ=TrC~\varphi={\operatorname{Tr}}_{\tilde{C}}. An application of theorem 6 then gives the conditions under which

χ⁡({p⁡(x),ρx})=χ⁡({p⁡(x),φ​ρx}).\chi(\{p(x),\rho_{x}\})=\chi(\{p(x),\varphi\rho_{x}\}).

Namely,

ρA​B~​C~=⨁jqj​∑xp⁡(x|j)​|x⟩​⟨x|A⊗(ρx)b~jL⊗ωb~jR​C~,\rho_{A\tilde{B}\tilde{C}}=\bigoplus_{j}q_{j}\sum_{x}p(x|j){{|{x}\rangle}\!{\langle{x}|}}_{A}\otimes(\rho_{x})_{\tilde{b}_{j}^{L}}\otimes\omega_{\tilde{b}_{j}^{R}\tilde{C}},

where p⁡(x|j)​qjp(x|j)q_{j} is the joint probability distribution for (x,j)(x,j) and ωb~jR​C~\omega_{\tilde{b}_{j}^{R}\tilde{C}} does not depend on xx. In the special case where φ\varphi corresponds to a measurement operation, the additional constraint [φ​ρx,φ​ρx′]=0[\varphi\rho_{x},\varphi\rho_{x^{\prime}}]=0 must hold because the output system is classical. Given the form of ρA​B~​C~\rho_{A\tilde{B}\tilde{C}}, this implies [(ρx)b~jL,(ρx′)b~jL]=0[(\rho_{x})_{\tilde{b}_{j}^{L}},(\rho_{x^{\prime}})_{\tilde{b}_{j}^{L}}]=0 and, in turn, that the states {ρx}\{\rho_{x}\} all commute. In the language of quantum information, we have found that the accessible information of an ensemble is equal to its Holevo quantity if and only if all the states in the ensemble commute. This condition for equality actually appeared in Holevo’s original paper [5].

VII Discussion

We have exhibited the explicit structure of the tripartite states ρA​B​C\rho_{ABC} which satisfy strong subadditivity with equality. Not only are they short quantum Markov chains in the sense of [1], it is even the case that the AA and CC systems are conditionally independent given BB, in a physically meaningful sense: there is information in the BB system which can be obtained by a non–demolition measurement, conditioned upon which the quantum state factorises.

By specialising our result to particular types of states, we can easily recover the entropic conditions for quantum error correction and the conditions for saturation in the Holevo bound. In the general case, our theorem characterises exactly when a quantum operation preserves correlations, whether they be classical, in the form of pure entanglement, or more exotic, such as combinations of the two or even bound entanglement [6].

We left open the problem of a similar characterisation in infinite dimension (of system BB — infinite AA and CC are covered by our result): we only note that our method will certainly not work, as it relies ultimately on the classification of finite dimensional operator algebras. A further interesting problem could be to address the approximate case: if a state almost satisfies strong subadditivity, does it mean that its structure is close in some sense to the form of theorem 6? There might be a relation to [2] (see remark 5), where an approximate fidelity condition was studied.

Appendix A An operator algebraic derivation of the Koashi–Imoto theorem

Let ρ1,…,ρK\rho_{1},\ldots,\rho_{K} be density operators on the finite–dimensional Hilbert space ℋ{\cal H}. We are interested in the quantum operations (completely positive, trace–perserving linear maps) T:ℬ⁡(ℋ)→ℬ⁡(ℋ)T:{\cal B}({\cal H})\rightarrow{\cal B}({\cal H}) which leave these states invariant:

∀kT​ρk=ρk.\forall k\quad T\rho_{k}=\rho_{k}. (17)

By possibly shrinking ℋ{\cal H} to the minimum joint supporting subspace of the ρk\rho_{k}, we may assume that the support of 1K​∑kρk\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k}\rho_{k} is ℋ{\cal H}, which we shall do in the following.

¿From the Stinespring dilation theorem [21] it follows that every such TT can be represented as

T​σ=Trℰ⁡(Uℋℰ​(σ⊗ε)​Uℋℰ∗),T\sigma={\operatorname{Tr}}_{\cal E}\bigl(U_{\cal HE}(\sigma\otimes\varepsilon)U_{\cal HE}^{*}\bigr), (18)

with another Hilbert space ℰ{\cal E}, a state ε\varepsilon on it, and a unitary acting on ℋ⊗ℰ{\cal H}\otimes{\cal E}.

In [7] the following result is proved by an explicit algorithmic construction:

Theorem 10 (Koashi, Imoto [7])

Associated to the states ρ1,…,ρK\rho_{1},\ldots,\rho_{K} there exists a decomposition of ℋ{\cal H} as

ℋ=⨁j𝒥j⊗𝒦j{\cal H}=\bigoplus_{j}{\cal J}_{j}\otimes{\cal K}_{j} (19)

into a direct sum of tensor products, such that:

11. The states ρk\rho_{k} decompose as

ρk=⨁jqj|k​ρj|k⊗ωj,\rho_{k}=\bigoplus_{j}q_{j|k}\rho_{j|k}\otimes\omega_{j},

where ρj|k\rho_{j|k} is a state on 𝒥j{\cal J}_{j}, ωj\omega_{j} is a state on 𝒦j{\cal K}_{j} (which is independent of kk), and (qj|k)j(q_{j|k})_{j} is a probability distribution over jj’s.

22. For every TT which leaves the ρk\rho_{k} invariant, every associated unitary from eq. (18) has the form

Uℋℰ=⨁k𝟙𝒥j⊗U𝒦j​ℰ,U_{\cal HE}=\bigoplus_{k}{\openone}_{{\cal J}_{j}}\otimes U_{{\cal K}_{j}{\cal E}},

with unitaries U𝒦j​ℰU_{{\cal K}_{j}{\cal E}} on 𝒦j⊗ℰ{\cal K}_{j}\otimes{\cal E} that satisfy

∀jTrℰ⁡(U𝒦j​ℰ​(ωj⊗ε)​U𝒦j​ℰ∗)=ωj.\forall j\quad{\operatorname{Tr}}_{\cal E}\bigl(U_{{\cal K}_{j}{\cal E}}(\omega_{j}\otimes\varepsilon)U_{{\cal K}_{j}{\cal E}}^{*}\bigr)=\omega_{j}.

The purpose of this appendix is to present a short (but non–constructive) proof of this theorem, based on the theory of operator algebras. Property 1 of the theorem has previously appeared in a paper of Lindblad [12] and our approach closely follows the one taken there.

We begin with a slight reformulation of the result, avoiding the environment system ℰ{\cal E}:

Proposition 11

In the above theorem, property 2 is equivalent to

2′2^{\prime}. For every TT which leaves the ρk\rho_{k} invariant,

∀jT|ℬ⁡(𝒥j⊗𝒦j)=id⊗Tj,\forall j\qquad T|_{{\cal B}({\cal J}_{j}\otimes{\cal K}_{j})}={\operatorname{id}}\otimes T_{j},

with id{\operatorname{id}} on 𝒥j{\cal J}_{j} and TjT_{j} on 𝒦j{\cal K}_{j} such that Tj​(ωj)=ωjT_{j}(\omega_{j})=\omega_{j}.

Proof . Clearly, 22 implies 2′2^{\prime}. In the other direction, consider any UU implementing TT. Clearly, because of 2′2^{\prime},

U|(𝒥j⊗𝒦j)​ℰ=𝟙𝒥j⊗U𝒦j​ℰ,U|_{({\cal J}_{j}\otimes{\cal K}_{j}){\cal E}}={\openone}_{{\cal J}_{j}}\otimes U_{{\cal K}_{j}{\cal E}},

which yields the form 22 for UU. □\Box

Proof of theorem 10. Consider the set of quantum operations

𝐅={F:∀k​F​ρk=ρk},{\bf F}=\bigl\{F:\forall k\ F\rho_{k}=\rho_{k}\bigr\},

which is obviously non–empty since it contains TT and id{\operatorname{id}}.

With each F∈𝐅F\in{\bf F} we associate the set

𝒜F={X∈ℬ⁡(ℋ):F∗​(X)=X}{\cal A}_{F}=\bigl\{X\in{\cal B}({\cal H}):F^{*}(X)=X\bigr\}

of operators left invariant by the adjoint map F∗F^{*}. By lemma 12 this is a ∗*–subalgebra of ℬ⁡(ℋ){\cal B}({\cal H}) and, in fact, if F∗​(X)=∑iBi∗​X​BiF^{*}(X)=\sum_{i}B_{i}^{*}XB_{i},

𝒜F={Bi,Bi∗}′={X:∀iXBi=BiX,XBi∗=Bi∗X}{\cal A}_{F}=\{B_{i},B_{i}^{*}\}^{\prime}=\{X:\forall i\ XB_{i}=B_{i}X,\ XB_{i}^{*}=B_{i}^{*}X\}

is the commutator of the Kraus operators of F∗F^{*}. By the same lemma, this algebra furthermore is the image of ℬ⁡(ℋ){\cal B}({\cal H}) under the projection map

P∗=limN→∞1N​∑n=1N(F∗)n,P^{*}=\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}(F^{*})^{n},

whose adjoint is

P=limN→∞1N​∑n=1NFn.P=\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}F^{n}.

Clearly, P∈𝐅P\in{\bf F}. Next, define

𝒜0=⋂F∈𝐅𝒜F,{\cal A}_{0}=\bigcap_{F\in{\bf F}}{\cal A}_{F},

which clearly is a ∗*–subalgebra itself. Because all dimensions are finite, it can actually be presented as a finite intersection

𝒜0=𝒜F1∩…∩𝒜FM,{\cal A}_{0}={\cal A}_{F_{1}}\cap\ldots\cap{\cal A}_{F_{M}},

and in fact there is F0∈𝐅F_{0}\in{\bf F} such that 𝒜0=𝒜F0{\cal A}_{0}={\cal A}_{F_{0}}. We may take, for example,

F0=1M​∑μ=1MFμF_{0}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{\mu=1}^{M}F_{\mu}

and use lemma 12. Denote the projection onto 𝒜0{\cal A}_{0} derived from F0∗F_{0}^{*} by P0∗P_{0}^{*}.

Lemma 13 gives us the form of 𝒜0{\cal A}_{0}:

𝒜0=⨁jℬ⁡(ℋbjL)⊗𝟙bjR,{\cal A}_{0}=\bigoplus_{j}{\cal B}({\cal H}_{b^{L}_{j}})\otimes{\openone}_{b^{R}_{j}},

and, likewise, of P0∗P_{0}^{*}:

P0​(ξ)=⨁jTrbjR⁡(Πj​ξ​Πj)⊗ωj.P_{0}(\xi)=\bigoplus_{j}{\operatorname{Tr}}_{b^{R}_{j}}\bigl(\Pi_{j}\xi\Pi_{j}\bigr)\otimes\omega_{j}.

ρk=P0​(ρk)=⨁jqj​ρj|k⊗ωj.\rho_{k}=P_{0}(\rho_{k})=\bigoplus_{j}q_{j}\rho_{j|k}\otimes\omega_{j}.

As for the properties of TT, because 𝒜T⊃𝒜0{\cal A}_{T}\supset{\cal A}_{0}, we have T∗|𝒜0=id𝒜0T^{*}|_{{\cal A}_{0}}={\operatorname{id}}_{{\cal A}_{0}}. More explicitly, for A∈ℬ⁡(𝒥j)A\in{\cal B}({\cal J}_{j}) and 𝟙∈ℬ⁡(𝒦j){\openone}\in{\cal B}({\cal K}_{j}),

T∗​(A⊗𝟙)=A⊗𝟙.T^{*}(A\otimes{\openone})=A\otimes{\openone}.

Now assume 0≤A≤𝟙0\leq A\leq{\openone}, and consider B∈ℬ⁡(𝒦j)B\in{\cal B}({\cal K}_{j}) such that 0≤B≤𝟙0\leq B\leq{\openone}. Then

0≤T∗​(A⊗B)≤T∗​(A⊗𝟙)=A⊗𝟙≤𝟙⊗𝟙.0\leq T^{*}(A\otimes B)\leq T^{*}(A\otimes{\openone})=A\otimes{\openone}\leq{\openone}\otimes{\openone}. (20)

This implies that T∗T^{*} maps ℬ⁡(𝒥j⊗𝒦j){\cal B}({\cal J}_{j}\otimes{\cal K}_{j}) into itself for all jj, and hence the same applies to TT.

Now, eq. (20) applied with the rank–one projector A=|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|A={{|{\psi}\rangle}\!{\langle{\psi}|}}, yields that

T∗​(|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|⊗B)=|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|⊗B′,T^{*}({{|{\psi}\rangle}\!{\langle{\psi}|}}\otimes B)={{|{\psi}\rangle}\!{\langle{\psi}|}}\otimes B^{\prime},

Here follow the general lemmas about unital completely positive maps which were used in the proof of theorem 10. The first one is a mean ergodic theorem for the dual of a quantum operation. (The statement is essentially the Kovács-Szűcs theorem — see e.g. [4], proposition 4.3.8 — but we give a proof in our setting.)

Lemma 12

For a quantum operation FF, the map

P∗=limN→∞1N​∑n=1N(F∗)nP^{*}=\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}(F^{*})^{n}

is a conditional expectation onto the ∗*–subalgebra

𝒜F={X:F∗​(X)=X}={Bi,Bi∗}′.{\cal A}_{F}=\{X:F^{*}(X)=X\}=\{B_{i},B_{i}^{*}\}^{\prime}.

Proof . First of all, we want to see that 𝒜F{\cal A}_{F} is a ∗*–subalgebra. It is a linear subspace and the Kraus representation shows that if F∗​(X)=XF^{*}(X)=X, then F∗​(X∗)=(F∗​(X))∗=X∗F^{*}(X^{*})=\bigl(F^{*}(X)\bigr)^{*}=X^{*}.

With this, the Schwarz inequality (see e.g. [4]) gives that for invariant XX,

F∗​(X∗​X)≥F∗​(X∗)​F∗​(X)=X∗​X.F^{*}(X^{*}X)\geq F^{*}(X^{*})F^{*}(X)=X^{*}X.

However, applying a faithful (i.e., non–degenenerate) invariant state, such as 1K​∑kρk\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k}\rho_{k}, leaves only the possibility of equality:

F∗​(X∗​X)=X∗​X,F^{*}(X^{*}X)=X^{*}X,

from which it follows straightforwardly that the product of invariant operators is again invariant.

For X∈𝒜FX\in{\cal A}_{F}, one can confirm by direct calculation that

∑i[X,Bi]∗​[X,Bi]=F∗​(X∗​X)−X∗​X=0,\sum_{i}[X,B_{i}]^{*}[X,B_{i}]=F^{*}(X^{*}X)-X^{*}X=0,

the latter by the previous observation that X∗​XX^{*}X is also invariant. But since the left hand side is a sum of positive terms, all of them must be 00, hence [X,Bi]=0[X,B_{i}]=0 for all ii. Similarly, [X,Bi∗]=0[X,B_{i}^{*}]=0 for all ii.

These facts together say that 𝒜F⊂{Bi,Bi∗}′{\cal A}_{F}\subset\{B_{i},B_{i}^{*}\}^{\prime}, while the opposite containment is trivial.

Another application of the Schwarz inequality gives that F∗F^{*} is a contraction. Hence the mean ergodic theorem for a contraction implies that the limit in the statement exists. (Due to the finite dimensional situation all the relevant topologies coincide.) To see P∗​(X)∈𝒜FP^{*}(X)\in{\cal A}_{F}, we compute

(F∗​P∗)​(X)−P∗​(X)=limN→∞1N​((F∗)N+1​(X)−F∗​(X)),(F^{*}P^{*})(X)-P^{*}(X)=\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\left((F^{*})^{N+1}(X)-F^{*}(X)\right)\!,

which is clearly 00 so the image of P∗P^{*} is contained in 𝒜F{\cal A}_{F}. Since P∗​(X)=XP^{*}(X)=X when X∈𝒜FX\in{\cal A}_{F}, it is also onto and a projection. □\Box

Lemma 13

Let 𝒜{\cal A} be a ∗*–subalgebra of ℬ⁡(ℋ){\cal B}({\cal H}), with a finite dimensional ℋ{\cal H}. Then there is a direct sum decomposition

ℋ=⨁jℋbjL⊗ℋbjR,{\cal H}=\bigoplus_{j}{\cal H}_{b^{L}_{j}}\otimes{\cal H}_{b^{R}_{j}},

such that

𝒜=⨁jℬ⁡(ℋbjL)⊗𝟙bjR.{\cal A}=\bigoplus_{j}{\cal B}\bigl({\cal H}_{b^{L}_{j}}\bigr)\otimes{\openone}_{b^{R}_{j}}.

Any completely positive and unital projection P∗P^{*} of ℬ⁡(ℋ){\cal B}({\cal H}) onto 𝒜{\cal A} is of the form

P∗​(X)=⨁jTrbjR⁡(Πj​X​Πj​(𝟙bjL⊗ωj))⊗𝟙bjR,P^{*}(X)=\bigoplus_{j}{\operatorname{Tr}}_{b^{R}_{j}}\bigl(\Pi_{j}X\Pi_{j}({\openone}_{b^{L}_{j}}\otimes\omega_{j})\bigr)\otimes{\openone}_{b^{R}_{j}},

Proof . See [22], section I.11. □\Box
